entities.name: Saint Cajetan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gaetano dei Conti di Thiene, canonized as Saint Cajetan, emerged as a pivotal figure in the Catholic Counter-Reformation, co-founding the Clerks Regular of the Divine Providence, commonly known as the Theatines, in 1524. Born in Vicenza, Republic of Venice, in 1480, Cajetan dedicated his life to reforming the clergy and renewing Christian piety amidst the burgeoning Protestant challenge and widespread moral decay within the Church. His efforts, alongside key collaborators like Gian Pietro Carafa (later Pope Paul IV), directly influenced the spiritual renewal that characterized the Council of Trent and the subsequent revitalization of Catholic life across Italy and beyond, particularly through the establishment of new, rigorous religious orders.

Following an early career in law and as a papal diplomat, Cajetan experienced a profound spiritual conversion around 1516, leading him to abandon secular pursuits for priestly ordination in 1517. Driven by a fervent desire to emulate the apostolic life and combat the laxity prevalent among the clergy, he founded the Oratory of Divine Love in Rome, a confraternity dedicated to prayer and charitable works. The foundational moment for his enduring legacy was the establishment of the Theatines on September 14, 1524, with Carafa and two other companions. This new order was unique: its members were priests who lived in community, took vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, and committed to intense pastoral work, including preaching, administering sacraments, and caring for the sick, without begging for alms – a stark contrast to many mendicant orders.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saint Cajetan's co-founding of the Theatines established a new model for clerical religious orders that profoundly influenced the Counter-Reformation, inspiring similar reforms and contributing to the spiritual renewal of the Catholic Church.
